subject: general
question: The power to legislate on 'Residuary Subjects' (matters not enumerated in any of the three Lists) rests exclusively with:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Parliament**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Residuary powers refer to the authority to legislate on matters not enumerated in the Union List, State List, or Concurrent List of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Under Article 248 of the Indian Constitution, Parliament has exclusive power to legislate on residuary subjects.
 
• This provision is supported by Entry 97 of the Union List in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution.
 
• Examples of residuary subjects include matters related to cyberspace, atomic energy, and other emerging technologies not envisioned at the time of drafting the Constitution.
 
• Unlike in federal systems like the USA, where residuary powers are given to the states, in India, these powers are vested in the central authority to ensure a strong and unified center.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• It contains three lists: Union List, State List, and Concurrent List, which define the distribution of powers between the Centre and States.
 
• Union List: Contains subjects of national importance (e.g., defense, foreign affairs).
 
• State List: Contains subjects of local or state-level importance (e.g., police, public health).
 
• Concurrent List: Contains subjects where both the Centre and States can legislate (e.g., education, marriage).
 
 
 
• **Article 248 of the Constitution:**
 
 
• It grants Parliament exclusive power to legislate on matters not enumerated in any of the three Lists.
 
• This ensures that emerging or unforeseen areas of legislation are uniformly governed across the country.
 
 
 
• **Residuary Powers in Federal Systems:**
 
 
• In India, residuary powers are vested in the Centre, unlike the USA, where they are given to the states.
 
• This reflects the quasi-federal nature of the Indian Constitution, prioritizing a strong central government.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Interpretation:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court of India has upheld the exclusive power of Parliament over residuary matters in several landmark cases.
 
• It ensures that no legislative vacuum exists in matters that may arise due to technological or societal advancements.
